title: Dynamic Memory Allocation on the Heap
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs test whether candidates can correctly allocate, index, and free heap memory with new/delete and avoid leaks or use-after-free.

phases.goal: Establish that heap storage is requested at run time with new, unlike compile-time-sized stack arrays.

must_hit.point: Heap memory is allocated dynamically: the amount is decided at run time, not at compile time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says the heap lets the program ask for storage sized by what it discovers while running, not a fixed compile-time size.

must_hit.point: A built-in array like int A[5] lives in the function stack frame with size fixed at compile time; new int[5] allocates a heap block and returns its address into a pointer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts A on the stack with p = new int[5] (or int* p = new int[5]) where p holds the heap block address.

must_hit.point: The pointer itself is a stack variable that holds the address of the heap block created by new[].
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes the stack-points-to-heap picture: p on the stack, the new[] block on the heap.

probes: How does allocating an array with new differ from declaring a built-in array like int A[5]?

hints.1: Think about when the size is known and where the storage lives.
hints.2: Compare a stack frame array fixed at compile time with an explicit new[] request whose address is stored in a pointer.
hints.3: int A[5] is on the stack at compile-time size; int* p = new int[5] puts a block of 5 ints on the heap and keeps its address in p.

phases.goal: Establish the full cycle: obtain with new[], use through the pointer, release with matching delete[], and null the pointer.

must_hit.point: A block obtained with new persists for as long as the program runs unless the program explicitly gives it back; releasing it is entirely the programmer's responsibility.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states heap lifetime is not automatic and delete (or delete[]) must be called by the programmer.

must_hit.point: An array allocated with new[] must be released with delete[]; after delete[] the pointer still holds the old address, which is no longer valid, so assign NULL to mark it as pointing nowhere.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes delete[] p; then p = NULL; and explains NULL as a deliberate points-to-nothing state versus a stale dangling address.

must_hit.point: A heap array reached through a pointer is indexed like an ordinary array: p[2] advances two elements past the address in p and accesses that value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows A[2] = 15 and p[2] = 15 side by side and says indexing is defined in terms of the pointer.

probes: After you allocate with new[], how do you correctly release the block, and what should you do with the pointer afterward?

hints.1: Heap memory is not cleaned up when a function returns the way stack locals are.
hints.2: Match new[] with delete[], then consider what address the pointer still holds.
hints.3: Call delete[] p to return the block, then set p = NULL so it is a null pointer rather than a dangling address.

phases.goal: Contrast automatic stack management and fixed compile-time size with manual heap ownership and run-time sizing.

must_hit.point: Stack memory is managed automatically—locals vanish when the function returns—whereas heap memory is not reclaimed automatically.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate clearly separates automatic stack lifetime from manual heap release.

must_hit.point: A stack array cannot be declared with a size known only at run time; the heap is the region that can satisfy a request whose size is discovered while the program runs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains that a user-supplied size rules out a compile-time stack array and requires new[].

probes: When would you choose heap allocation with new[] over a built-in stack array?

hints.1: Consider lifetime management and when the size becomes known.
hints.2: Stack: automatic reclaim, fixed compile-time size. Heap: manual release, size can be decided at run time.
hints.3: Use the heap when size comes from input at run time; accept that you must delete[] yourself because the heap is not reclaimed automatically.

phases.goal: Apply new[] to a run-time-sized array and recognize the leak when reallocating without delete[].

must_hit.point: A typical pattern reads size from the user, then allocates with int* p = new int[size] because that size is known only at run time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate sketches cin >> size followed by new int[size] and notes a stack array could not use that bound.

must_hit.point: If you later allocate a fresh block with another new int[size] and assign it to p, the first block must be released with delete[] before reassigning or it is leaked.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate flags that p = new int[size] a second time orphans the old block unless delete[] ran first.

probes: Walk through allocating an array whose length the user enters, then changing that length later—what can go wrong?

hints.1: The interesting case is when size is not a compile-time constant.
hints.2: Allocate with new int[size] after reading size; think carefully before a second new[] into the same pointer.
hints.3: Before p = new int[size] again, delete[] the first block; otherwise the old heap memory stays reserved and unused—a leak.

tradeoffs.topic: Stack array vs heap array with new[]
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A built-in stack array has compile-time-fixed size and vanishes automatically when the function returns. A heap array from new[] can use a size discovered at run time and persists until the programmer releases it with delete[]; the pointer on the stack only holds the address.

tradeoffs.topic: Leaving a pointer after delete[] vs setting it to NULL
tradeoffs.strong_answer: After delete[], the pointer still holds the old address, which is no longer valid. Assigning NULL makes a recognisable null pointer that points nowhere, instead of leaving a dangling stale address.

gotchas.correction: The heap block stays reserved and unusable for the rest of the program's life—a memory leak—because heap memory is never reclaimed automatically.

gotchas.trap: Using the pointer after delete[] without resetting it
gotchas.correction: The old address is no longer valid; accessing it reaches memory the program no longer owns. Set the pointer to NULL after delete[].

gotchas.trap: Reassigning p = new int[size] to resize without deleting the first block
gotchas.correction: The second new[] replaces the pointer with a brand-new block and orphans the first; delete[] the first block before reassigning or it is leaked.
